chunks: He said: Abu Ubaidullah Muhammad ibn Imran al-Marzbani reported to me, saying: Hanzalah Abu Ghassan narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Mundhir Hisham ibn Muhammad ibn al-Saib narrated to us, from Muhraz, from Ja’far the freed-slave of Abu Huraira, who said:

Artat ibn Suhaiyya entered upon Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan when one hundred and thirty years had already passed over him. Abd al-Malik said to him: What remains of your poetry, O Artat? He replied: By Allah, O Commander of the Faithful, I no longer rejoice, nor get angry, nor drink, and poetry only comes to me through these impulses. However, I am the one who composed: I have seen man devoured by the nights * as the earth devours fallen scraps of iron / And death, when it comes, leaves nothing * upon the soul of the son of Adam as surplus / And I know that it will keep returning until * it fulfills its pledge with Abu al-Walid.

The narrator said: Abd al-Malik was alarmed, for his kunya was Abu al-Walid. So Artat said to him: I only meant myself, O Commander of the Faithful — for Artat’s kunya was also Abu al-Walid. Then Abd al-Malik said: And I too, by Allah, what passes with you shall pass with me.
May Allah bless our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and his family, and grant them peace.

key_terms.أمير المؤمنين: Commander of the Faithful, the title of the caliph
key_terms.المنيّة: Death personified, keeping its pledge and sparing no one
key_terms.شعر: Poetry, which in classical Arab thought requires emotional impulse to compose
key_terms.كنية (أبو الوليد): Honorific patronymic (kunya) shared by both Artat and the caliph, central to the dramatic irony

ai.seo_question: What did the aged poet Artat ibn Suhaiyya tell Caliph Abd al-Malik about death?
ai.summary: This narration recounts the visit of Artat ibn Suhaiyya, a poet who had reached 130 years of age, to the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. When asked about his poetry, Artat explains that old age has stripped him of the emotions that inspire verse, yet he still composed lines about death’s inevitability. The poem inadvertently alarms the caliph, whose kunya Abu al-Walid matches the name in the verse. Artat reassures him that he meant himself, but the caliph acknowledges that death will claim him too. The anecdote illustrates the universal reality of mortality transcending age and power.

en.mulla-asgharali-m-m-jaffer: 10. He said: Abu Ubaidullah Muhammad ibn Imran al-Marzbani reported to me from Hanzalah Abu Ghassan, who reported from Abu al-Mundhar Hisham ibn Muhammad ibn al-Saeb, from Muhraz, from Ja’far, the client of Abu Huraira, who said:

Once, Artat ibn Suhaiyya, who was then one hundred thirty years old, called upon Abdul Malik ibn Marwan. Abdul Malik said: "O Artat! What is now left of your poetry?" He said: "By Allah, O, Commander of the faithfuls, I do not rejoice, nor do I get angry, nor do I drink. And if I feel like expressing these sentiments in a poem, then nothing comes to my mind but the following: "I have seen man devoured by the nights, the way iron junk is eaten up by the earth; And when death arrives, it does not leave for the Adam’s son, any extras or surplus. And I know that it will continue to come, Till it fulfills its pledge with Abul Al-Walid."

Abdul Malik’s kunya was Abul Al-Walid, so when he heard the couplet, he was terribly shaken. So, Artat said: "I meant myself, O, Commander of the faithfuls." Because Artat also had the kunya Abu Al-Walid. Abdul Malik said: "By Allah, whatever happens to you shall happen to me also."
And may Allah bless our master Muhammad the Prophet, the unlearned, and his progeny.
